Capabilities and frames

The seam between Faber and every way an operating system can implement I/O.

call is Faber's low-level capability call primitive — the boundary between Faber code and the outside world. It opens a typed conversation (channel) with a host resource identified by a route string, then exchanges structured frames (frame) over directional half-streams. The runtime dispatches each route to the native leaf that serves it, and that leaf implements the actual I/O — filesystem, networking, console, time, randomness, or anything else the OS can do.

The call primitive#

call is a keyword, not a function. It opens an opaque conversation with a route named by an ascii literal and optional opener data:

main {
    # Simple materialized call: open, send opener, drain response
    let string content ← call 'solum:lege' ("config.toml") ↦ string

    # Typed conversation handle for streaming interaction
    let channel s ← call 'processus:exsequi' ("ls -la")
}

The route string follows a prefix:verb pattern. Dispatch matches on the prefix — the leaf that owns a prefix handles all verbs under it:

solum:lege   ─┐
solum:scribe ─┼─►  prefix "solum"  ──►  filesystem leaf
solum:crea   ─┘

call is not a foreign function interface. It does not call C functions, load dynamic libraries, or embed inline assembly. It is a structured message passing boundary: Faber sends typed frames and receives typed frames, without knowing whether the answering side runs in-process, delegates to a system call, or forwards to a remote host.

Frame types#

Five compiler-owned types form the frame system:

TypeRoleKey surface
channelConversation handle — an in-flight bidirectional exchangeCreated by call; drained via ↦ T or split into views
frame<T>Frame envelope — one structured message in a conversationFields: id, call, status, data, created_ms, from, trace
statusLifecycle marker enumrequest, item, byte, bulk, done, error, cancel
send<T>Outbound half-stream — send frames to the providerda(T), fini() → status
recv<T>Inbound half-stream — receive frames from the provideraccipe(), cursor(), exhauri(), fini()

Using directional views#

main {
    # Open a conversation, get directional views
    let channel s ← call 'solum:scribe' ("output.txt")
    let send<string> out ← s.send<string>()
    let recv<string> input ← s.recv<string>()

    # Send content frames
    out.da("line one")
    out.da("line two")
    out.fini()

    # Read response frames
    for from input.cursor() let frame {
        print frame.data
    }
    let status inbound ← input.fini()
}

Simple materialization#

For the common case — open, send opener, drain all response frames into one value — channel ↦ T collapses the conversation:

main {
    # Read a file: open + drain into string
    let string body ← call 'solum:lege' ("config.toml") ↦ string

    # Collect the inbound frames into a list
    let list<string> lines ← call 'solum:lege' ("data.txt") ↦ list<string>
}

Materialization uses a type-directed collector: ↦ string concatenates all inbound frames, and ↦ list<T> collects frames into a list.

Native leaves#

Each effect family is served by a native leaf in the faber-leaf crate (crates/faber-leaf). The interpreter (faber run) and generated Rust share it. Each leaf owns all verbs under its prefix:

LeafPrefixI/O domain
filesystemonly:*Read, write, metadata, directory operations
stdioconsolum:*Console I/O: stdin, stdout, stderr
processprocessus:*Process execution, environment, working directory
clocktempus:*Time: now, monotonic, sleep
entropyaleator:*Randomness: floats, integers, bytes, uuid
tcpcaelum:*TCP listen, connect, accept, read, write
httphttp:*HTTP client calls
websocketwebsocket:*WebSocket connect, accept, send, receive

A route that no leaf serves is refused at run time. Faber code can also answer a route itself with an @ call 'prefix:name' handler on a top-level function.

Layer stack#

Faber source:     call 'solum:lege' (path) ↦ string
Compiler:         channel open + generic attach (no leaf crate names)
Runtime:          route lookup + conversation protocol
Leaf:             the filesystem leaf reads the file, returns content

The compiler emits generic dispatch — it never embeds leaf crate names into generated code. Source names a route; the runtime decides which leaf answers it.

Norma wrappers#

Most Faber code does not call call directly. The Norma standard library wraps common call routes in typed functions:

# A typed wrapper over an call route (Norma's own wrappers also declare
# a fault channel for I/O failures)
fn exsequi(string command) → string {
    return call 'processus:exsequi' (command) ↦ string
}

These wrapper functions provide type safety, documentation, and error handling without hiding the fact that I/O crosses the call boundary. The Norma wrappers live under lib/norma/src/.
